title: Starting a Hospice Program in Florida: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

html:
Introduction

Starting a Hospice Program in Florida represents a meaningful opportunity to serve terminally ill individuals and their families while building a compliant, sustainable care business. This vital service focuses on palliative care, comfort, and dignity at the end of life. Oversight and funding are administered by the Florida Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through the AHCA Division of Medicaid and the Statewide Medicaid Managed Care (SMMC) programs, as well as the federal Medicare program.

With a large and aging population creating substantial growth opportunities, and reimbursement rates for routine home care ranging from $162 to $241 per day, Florida offers a well-established yet competitive market for providers prepared to navigate its unique regulatory landscape. The primary challenge and gatekeeper for market entry is the state’s Certificate of Need (CON) process, which governs the establishment and expansion of hospice services to ensure controlled growth and maintain high-quality standards.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice Program in Florida, from understanding the complex CON and AHCA regulations to staffing your interdisciplinary team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Florida’s Hospice Program Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Florida’s Hospice Program Regulations

Florida regulates Hospice Programs through the Florida Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA), specifically the Bureau of Health Facility Regulation’s Long-Term Care Services Unit. AHCA is responsible for regulating licensed hospice services under Florida Statutes Chapter 400, Part IV, which includes overseeing the critical Certificate of Need (CON) process that governs licensing and expansion, ensuring controlled access and maintaining quality standards. This CON requirement is the single most important regulatory hurdle for new providers, as a license cannot be granted without first demonstrating need and receiving CON approval for a specific geographic service area.

Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations must also comply with federal hospice conditions of participation as defined by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). The regulatory framework in Florida emphasizes a patient- and family-centered approach prioritizing comfort, dignity, and quality of life. Key compliance areas include the development and maintenance of an individualized plan of care, robust documentation, adherence to patient rights, and rigorous quality oversight. Licenses are issued by AHCA and typically require renewal every two years (biennially).

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While Florida issues a single “Hospice License,” providers deliver care through several distinct service levels, each with different staffing, operational, and reimbursement implications. Understanding these is key to designing your service model and business plan.

Florida supports multiple hospice service levels, including:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): The most common level of care, provided wherever the patient calls home, including private residences, nursing homes, or assisted living facilities. This involves intermittent visits from the interdisciplinary team.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of medical crisis to manage acute symptoms. This level requires more intensive, round-the-clock nursing care in the patient’s home to avoid hospitalization.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): Short-term care provided in a Medicare-certified hospital, skilled nursing facility, or dedicated inpatient hospice facility for pain or symptom management that cannot be handled in another setting.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term inpatient care provided to the patient to give their primary caregivers a temporary rest. This is limited to five consecutive days at a time.

Program size is typically measured by patient census and staffing capacity. Caseloads are managed based on staffing ratios, such as 1 nurse to 8 patients for routine home care. Demand is strongest in the densely populated southeastern metropolitan regions such as Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach counties. In contrast, rural northern counties may offer entry opportunities with less competition, though referral networks may be more challenging to build.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can serve patients, you must establish a sound legal and business foundation. Providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or Corporation. The licensing process in Florida is a multi-stage endeavor, beginning long before the formal application is submitted.

First, you must complete these foundational business steps:

  • Register your business entity with the Florida Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability and professional liability (malpractice) insurance.
  • Establish a financial foundation and prepare statements demonstrating fiscal viability, a key component of both the CON and licensure applications.

Next, you must navigate Florida’s rigorous licensing pathway:

  • Certificate of Need (CON) Application: This is the first and most challenging step. You must submit a Letter of Intent and then a detailed application to AHCA demonstrating an unmet need for hospice services in your proposed service area. This is a competitive process that occurs during specific batching cycles.
  • Licensing Application: Only after receiving CON approval can you submit a formal licensing application (AHCA Form 3110-4001) to AHCA. This includes your CON approval letter, detailed policies and procedures, proof of financial stability, and background screening for all leadership.
  • Pre-Licensure Inspection: AHCA will conduct an unannounced on-site survey to ensure your operations, policies, and (if applicable) facility meet all state and federal requirements before a license is issued.

Licensing timelines are extensive. The CON process itself can take over a year. Once a CON is secured, the AHCA licensing application review and approval process generally ranges from 8 to 10 months, depending on your readiness and the completeness of your submission.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is essential for securing funding and navigating the financial complexities of the CON and licensure process. Startup costs in Florida typically range from $200,000 to $750,000, with the higher end reflecting the cost of building or leasing a dedicated inpatient hospice facility.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by your interdisciplinary team, with staffing representing approximately 60-70% of total costs. Your financial projections must be grounded in the state’s reimbursement structure.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges for FY 2024 include:

  • Routine Home Care: Approximately $162 – $241 per day, depending on the length of stay.
  • Continuous Home Care: Reimbursed at an hourly rate, which can equate to over $1,400 per day.
  • General Inpatient Care: Daily rates can exceed $1,100.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Reimbursed at a daily rate of approximately $481.

These rates are primarily set by Medicare and adopted by Florida Medicaid and managed care organizations. With strong operational management and consistent referrals, providers operating at 85% to 95% of their staffed capacity can generally achieve profit margins in the 8% to 12% range. New providers typically reach a break-even point within 12 to 18 months of becoming fully operational.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

While most hospice care is delivered in the patient’s home, your agency needs a compliant administrative office. If you plan to offer General Inpatient Care in your own facility, it must meet stringent physical plant requirements.

For inpatient hospice facilities, AHCA and CMS requirements include:

  • A minimum of 2,500 square feet.
  • Full compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).
  • Strict adherence to fire safety and local building codes.
  • Patient bedrooms must be at least 120 square feet for a single occupant.
  • A minimum of 1 bathroom for every 3 patient rooms.

Your administrative office, even without an inpatient component, must be accessible, secure, and have adequate space for confidential record-keeping, staff meetings, and supply storage. Location selection for either type of space should consider zoning laws, accessibility for staff and families, proximity to major hospitals and referral sources, and the availability of a qualified clinical workforce.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Hospice care is delivered by a mandated interdisciplinary group (IDG) that works together to create and manage the patient’s plan of care. Hiring a compassionate, qualified, and compliant team is non-negotiable.

Required roles for a Florida hospice typically include:

  • Administrator: A full-time position, preferably with a Bachelor’s degree and at least two years of supervisory experience in hospice or a related healthcare field.
  • Medical Director: A licensed physician responsible for the medical component of the hospice’s patient care program.
  • Registered Nurses (RNs): Serve as case managers and provide skilled nursing care.
  • Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs): Provide nursing care under the supervision of an RN.
  • Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs) / Hospice Aides: Assist with personal care and daily living activities.
  • Medical Social Workers (MSWs): Address psychosocial needs and connect patients and families with community resources.
  • Spiritual Counselors / Chaplains: Provide spiritual support aligned with the patient’s and family’s beliefs.
  • Bereavement Counselors: Offer grief and loss support to the family for up to a year after the patient’s death.
  • Volunteers: A critical component, providing companionship, respite for caregivers, and administrative support.

Training is heavily regulated. All direct care staff must complete an initial 40 hours of training before providing patient care. This must cover topics such as hospice principles (16 hrs), infection control (8 hrs), communication skills (8 hrs), and specialized care needs (8 hrs). Additionally, all staff must complete 12 hours of ongoing continuing education annually to stay current on best practices and regulatory changes.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your operational rulebook is your set of policies and procedures. A comprehensive, well-written policy manual is required for licensure and is the first thing surveyors will review during an inspection. Deficiencies in this area are a common reason for delays and citations.

Florida requires written policies covering all aspects of your operation, including:

  • Patient Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Individualized Plan of Care (IPC) Development, Review, and Update
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Staffing Plans, Training, and Supervision
  • Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Planning
  • Bereavement Care Services for Families
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI)
  • Volunteer Program Management
  • Ethical Conduct and Corporate Compliance

Central to hospice care is the Individualized Plan of Care (IPC). This document must be developed by the interdisciplinary group in collaboration with the patient and family. It must be meticulously documented and reviewed regularly—at least every 15 days for patients receiving continuous or inpatient care, and every 60 days for those on routine care.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike many consumer-facing businesses, hospice marketing is not about direct-to-consumer advertising. Success depends entirely on building a strong network of professional referral sources. Your reputation for quality, compliance, and responsiveness is your most powerful marketing tool.

Referrals for hospice services in Florida typically come from:

  • Hospitals (discharge planners, case managers, and palliative care teams)
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (Directors of Nursing and social workers)
  • Assisted Living Facilities
  • Oncologists and other specialist physicians
  • Primary care physicians
  • Home health agencies

Successful providers focus their efforts on building trust within the local healthcare ecosystem. This involves meeting with case managers, providing educational in-services on the benefits of hospice, and demonstrating excellent clinical outcomes and communication. A compliant, well-run agency that makes the referral process smooth and reliable for its partners will see a steady stream of patients.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Achieving licensure is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Your hospice will be subject to ongoing oversight and unannounced inspections.

Oversight includes surveys from AHCA’s Bureau of Health Facility Regulation for state compliance and the CMS Atlanta Regional Office (or its contracted accrediting organization) for Medicare certification. Inspections are comprehensive and focus on every aspect of your operation, from patient charts to personnel files and infection control practices.

Common deficiencies cited during Florida hospice surveys include:

  • Documentation Issues (40%): Incomplete or untimely Individualized Plans of Care, missing signatures, or inadequate visit notes.
  • Policy Deficiencies (25%): Outdated policies or failure to follow established procedures.
  • Financial Concerns (20%): Issues related to billing, eligibility verification, or fiscal management.
  • Leadership/Staffing Issues (15%): Inadequate staffing levels, incomplete training records, or missing background screenings.

To avoid these pitfalls, you must embed a culture of continuous quality improvement. This means conducting regular internal audits, staying current on regulatory changes, and ensuring your documentation is always audit-ready.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to open a Hospice Program in Florida?

The timeline is significant due to the Certificate of Need (CON) process, which can take a year or more. After securing a CON, the AHCA licensing application, review, and pre-licensure survey can take another 8-10 months. New providers typically achieve break-even operations within 12 to 18 months of becoming operational.

What licenses are required?

You need a Hospice License from the Florida Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA). Critically, you must first obtain a Certificate of Need (CON) for your specific geographic service area before you can even apply for the license. This makes Florida one of the more challenging states in which to start a new hospice.

What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement primarily comes from Medicare and Medicaid, which pay a per diem (daily) rate. For FY 2024, daily rates range from $162-$241 for routine home care, with significantly higher rates available for higher levels of care like continuous home care, general inpatient care (up to $1,466 per day), and respite care.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice Program in Florida is a complex but deeply rewarding venture. It requires careful planning to navigate the formidable Certificate of Need process, a deep understanding of AHCA and CMS regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. Providers who invest in building a foundation of compliance, hiring a compassionate and qualified team, and cultivating strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and will make a profound impact on the lives of patients and families across the state.
